summary:
Legal gender recognition in Iceland rests on the 2019 self-determination law, which took effect on 1 January 2020 and was implemented in January 2021. It permits legal gender change with no restrictions, makes an X third-gender marker available, allows minors to change their legal gender with parental consent, and prohibits medical interventions on intersex children against their will except where health-related. Non-binary identity is recognised in law.

Anti-discrimination and hate-crime law covers both sexual orientation and gender identity. Amendments to the Penal Code in 1996 made it illegal to publicly attack a person or group with mockery, defamation, abuse or threats because of their sexual orientation, and a 2014 amendment added gender identity to the anti-discrimination grounds. Discrimination is illegal, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and bathroom access is protected. Conversion therapy is banned; the 2023 measure passed 53 to 0 with three abstentions.

Relationship and family recognition is settled. Same-sex marriage is recognised, following a unanimous 49 to 0 parliamentary vote in 2010. Stepchild adoption has been permitted since 2000, and from 27 June 2006 same-sex couples gained equal access to joint adoption and publicly funded IVF insemination. Registered partnerships, available from 1996, already carried many of the same rights and benefits as marriage, including stepchild adoption.

Reporting and redress routes exist. The national emergency service, 112, defines hate crime as offences committed from prejudice or hatred and publishes guidance for victims alongside reporting routes; it states that queer people are more likely to be victims of violence. Police-recorded potential hate crimes numbered 16 in 2023, triple the figure for the previous year, 11 in 2024, and 7 in the year to date when the report was published. The queer rights group Samtökin 78 has called for stronger hate-crime legislation. The Equality Complaints Committee is the official mechanism for discrimination complaints.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal nationwide for men and women. Outright International describes Iceland's laws as progressive while noting acknowledged gaps in protection. Equaldex ranks Iceland first of 121 jurisdictions for gay and lesbian people at 93 per cent, and records gender change with no restrictions, non-binary recognition, hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, a full ban on intersex infant surgery, a conversion therapy ban and protected bathroom access. That index measures conditions for gay and lesbian people rather than trans people specifically. UK travel advice states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in law, and provides dedicated LGBT+ guidance for visitors.
tangentialFactors:
Iceland's legal trajectory runs from criminalisation to protection. Section 178 of the Penal Code criminalised same-sex relations between 1869 and 1940, and public antipathy towards LGBT people remained high until the 1980s; some of the earliest Icelanders to come out publicly, Hörður Torfason and Anna Kristjánsdottir, initially faced discrimination and ridicule. The 1996 anti-discrimination amendments, the 2010 marriage vote and the 2023 conversion therapy ban mark the reversal. The 2019 self-determination process replaced an earlier law that had itself been among Europe's most progressive.

A blood donation restriction on men who have sex with men was challenged by a lawsuit in 2014, relaxed to a four-month deferral in September 2021, and is lifted entirely from September 2026.

Public expression is visible. Reykjavík Pride drew about 100,000 people in 2015, roughly 30 per cent of the population, and in 2016 President Guðni Th. Jóhannesson became the first president to attend a gay pride parade. Bars and cafés serving a gay clientele are concentrated in Reykjavík; outside the capital the sparse population means there is almost no gay scene, and Akureyri has no gay bars.

The age of consent was set at 14 in 1992 and raised to 15 in 2007, regardless of gender or sexual orientation. A 2000 Gallup poll found 53 per cent of Icelanders supported lesbian and gay adoption rights, with 35 per cent against.
localsOnly:
Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in education has been illegal since 2008. Since 2016 the town of Hafnarfjörður has included information about same-sex relationships in its eighth-grade sex education lessons for pupils aged 14 to 15, and the Queer Student Association of Iceland runs social activities and field trips for University of Iceland students.

LGBTI organisations can register in Iceland. Trans Ísland and other activists have mapped the challenges that remain after the 2019 self-determination reform.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Equaldex ranking is an index of conditions for gay and lesbian people and does not measure trans-specific conditions. Its 93 per cent score and first-place ranking should be read on that basis.

Police-recorded hate crime figures are raw counts of potential hate crimes, are not disaggregated by the group targeted, and are small in absolute terms; they do not establish a trans-specific risk rate.

The OSCE hate crime pages on Iceland's legislation and national frameworks produced no usable findings, and the Pink Iceland page for trans and non-binary travellers likewise produced no usable finding.

Outright International refers to acknowledged gaps in protection without specifying them. The 2019 Reykjavík Grapevine piece predates the implementation of the self-determination law and does not itemise the challenges it attributes to activists.
